summary: This Standards Track document defines how to use ML-DSA, a post-quantum digital signature scheme from NIST FIPS 204, within JOSE (JSON) and COSE (CBOR) formats.

eli5.summary: There is a new signature style that should hold up against future super-computers. This explains how to write it in the two common signed-message formats.

questions: post-quantum signatures in jwt and cbor
what is the akp key type
how big is an ml-dsa signature
subtitle: How to sign JSON and CBOR messages with ML-DSA, a signature scheme designed to resist future quantum computers.

tldr.problem: JOSE (JSON) and COSE (CBOR) had no registered way to carry ML-DSA, the post-quantum digital signature scheme from NIST FIPS 204, or to express its keys.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a generic Algorithm Key Pair (AKP) key type with pub and priv parameters, registers ML-DSA-44, ML-DSA-65 and ML-DSA-87 as algorithms, and fixes the private key to a 32-byte seed.
tldr.outcome: Applications can now put ML-DSA keys and signatures in JWS, JWK, COSE_Sign and COSE_Key formats, at the cost of much larger keys and signatures than traditional algorithms.

today: RFC 9964 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2026. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, and it obsoletes and updates none itself.

sections.title: What the RFC Adds
sections.content:
RFC 9964 explains how to use ML-DSA keys and signatures, as described in NIST FIPS 204, together with JOSE (JSON Object Signing and Encryption) and COSE (CBOR Object Signing and Encryption). ML-DSA is the Module-Lattice-Based Digital Signature Standard, a Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) signature scheme.

The RFC does two things. It defines a new key type called Algorithm Key Pair (AKP) that can hold public and private keys for algorithms beyond the ones registered here. It also defines a thumbprint procedure for AKP keys, so they can be compared using the methods of RFC 7638 and RFC 9679.
sections.eli5: There is a new kind of secret signature stamp. This RFC says how to describe the stamp in two popular message formats so everyone writes it down the same way.

sections.title: The AKP Key Type
sections.content:
An AKP key holds public and private information as byte strings, in a format that the alg value specifies. The idea of public and private information classes comes from Section 8.1 of RFC 7517.

  • The alg parameter (a JWK parameter or COSE Key common parameter) is REQUIRED for every AKP key.
  • The pub parameter carries the public information and is REQUIRED.
  • The priv parameter carries the private information and MUST NOT be present in public keys.

In a JWK the byte strings are base64url encoded. In a COSE key no encoding is needed, because CBOR carries raw bytes. In JOSE the key type is AKP; in COSE it is the integer 7, with pub at label -1 and priv at label -2.
sections.eli5: An AKP key is a labelled box with a slot for the public half of a key and, only if it is a secret copy, a slot for the private half. The label says which algorithm the key belongs to.

sections.title: Private Keys Are Seeds
sections.content:
NIST FIPS 204 describes two forms of an ML-DSA private key: a seed, and a private key expanded from that seed. This RFC supports only the seed. It says the seed gives one compact representation that is the same in COSE and JOSE, which simplifies key management and reduces storage.

For these algorithms the priv parameter MUST be the seed and MUST be 32 bytes long. The RFC contrasts this with RFC 9881, which supports the expanded format to maximize interoperability with existing implementations. Here the expanded format is intentionally left out so there is a single representation.
sections.eli5: Instead of carrying around a huge secret key, you carry a small starting number from which the big key can always be rebuilt. Everyone agrees to share only that small number.

sections.title: The Three ML-DSA Algorithms
sections.content:
ML-DSA comes in security levels. The RFC registers three algorithm names, ML-DSA-44, ML-DSA-65 and ML-DSA-87, using the parameter choices in Table 1 of FIPS 204. The pub parameter is the public key as described in Section 5.3 of FIPS 204, and signatures are produced as in Algorithm 2 of FIPS 204 and encoded as byte strings per Section 7.2.

The ctx parameter MUST be the empty string for all three. In a JSON Web Signature the signature bytes are base64url encoded, so the encoded form is larger than the sizes in the table. In COSE no encoding is needed.

The RFC warns that ML-DSA produces significantly larger public keys and signatures than traditional algorithms. That can be a problem with limited bandwidth, memory or processing capacity, and ML-DSA may not suit use cases that need small keys or signatures. Using thumbprints can reduce the need to repeat public key representations.
sections.eli5: There are small, medium and large versions of the stamp, and the bigger ones are harder to forge. All of them leave much bigger marks than old-style stamps, so they take more room on the page.

sections.title: AKP Thumbprints
sections.content:
AKP keys and their thumbprints are not tied to ML-DSA; they suit other algorithms too. A thumbprint is a short identifier computed from a key's required parameters.

For a COSE Key Thumbprint (RFC 9679) the required AKP parameters are kty (label 1, value 7), alg (label 3) and pub (label -1, a byte string). For a JWK Thumbprint (RFC 7638) they are kty, alg and pub, which in lexicographic order are alg, kty, pub. The kid values in the RFC's examples show such thumbprints.
sections.eli5: A thumbprint is a short nickname made from the important parts of a key, so two people can check they mean the same key without comparing the whole thing.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 7515, RFC 7517 and RFC 9053 apply. A detailed analysis of ML-DSA is out of scope; the RFC points to FIPS 204 and to the considerations in RFC 9881, including randomized versus deterministic signing.

  • Key compromise: the seed and the private key expanded from it need the same protection. Whoever gets either can forge signatures.
  • No HashML-DSA: the RFC does not specify HashML-DSA (Section 5.4 of FIPS 204). Because the verify routines differ, supporting it later would need additional algorithm registrations.
  • Key validation: when an AKP algorithm requires or encourages validation, all algorithm-related parameters MUST be validated. For these algorithms the seed length check MUST be performed; the seed is 256 bits, or 32 bytes.
  • Mismatched parameters: if public and private parameters were tampered with or mismatched, the consequences range from failed operations to private key compromise.
sections.eli5: If a thief gets your secret starting number, they can sign things as you, so guard it. Also check that the two halves of a key really belong together before you use them.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA has registered the new algorithms, key types and key parameters in both worlds. In COSE, ML-DSA-44, ML-DSA-65 and ML-DSA-87 take the values -48, -49 and -50 in the COSE Algorithms registry, each marked Recommended: Yes. The AKP key type is value 7 in COSE Key Types, with pub at label -1 and priv at label -2, both byte strings.

In JOSE, the three algorithms are added to the JSON Web Signature and Encryption Algorithms registry with JOSE Implementation Requirements of Optional. AKP is added to JSON Web Key Types (also Optional), and pub and priv are added to JSON Web Key Parameters for the AKP key type, with information classes Public and Private.
sections.eli5: The official list keeper wrote the new names and numbers into the two big phone books so nobody else uses them for something different.
